notes.why: Dim light and bright light (Hess 1923): in near darkness the field leans toward the bright side and in ordinary light it leans away. Easy; the draft's thresholds are invented.

A sudden fall in brightness (a third within a third of a second) closes the field to a point and reopens it over two or three seconds, as a fan worm withdraws (Bok 2017). Needs a brightness trigger the engine lacks.
A mole digging: a low rumble raises and brightens the field, as an earthworm surfaces (Catania 2008). Needs the microphone's low band, with consent.
A leech's body of eyes: with the phone flat and face up, the top half leans green and the bottom half blue (Stowasser 2019). Needs zones and device orientation.
The draft proposes separate millipede and centipede views; until they exist the word table sends them here.

rows: An earthworm has no eyes. Light-sensitive cells lie in the skin of every segment, most of them at the head and the tail, and tiny windows in a layer of pigment let light reach them from set directions.
An earthworm crawls away from ordinary light, but it moves toward light that is very dim.

Florida earthworms rush out of their burrows when the ground carries the vibration of a digging mole. Bait collectors copy it by scraping a stake driven into the soil, and worms come up as far as 12 metres away.

A medicinal leech has five pairs of eyecups on its head and seven pairs of light-sensing spots in every segment of its body. The spots on its back respond best to green light, and those underneath to ultraviolet.

Each cup-shaped eye of a freshwater planarian samples the world about every 35 degrees, and behaviour tests on another planarian give the same coarse sharpness. Planarians flee ultraviolet light most strongly, and worms without eyes, or without heads, still flee near-ultraviolet light. Land planarians, such as the hammerhead worms, have many tiny eyes on the head.

Fan worms and Christmas tree worms have eyes on their feathery tentacles. Their light-sensing pigment peaks at 464 nanometres, close to the blue light of a shallow reef, and a passing shadow makes them pull back into their tubes at once.

Worms meet most of the world through touch, taste and moisture. A leech's skin answers vibration up to about 50 times a second, and land planarians need damp ground to live. None of this reaches a camera.

This view shows only how much light there is, where it comes from and how it changes. It weights blue light most, because planarians and the underside of a leech answer ultraviolet most strongly and blue is the nearest colour the camera records. The weighting is the app's own choice.
With &draw=shadow, a sudden fall of light, as when a shadow passes, sends a dark ring across the picture. The ring is the app's drawing.

shadow.note: how dark the ring is when the light falls

rows.title: No eyes
rows.text: If you are a nightcrawler, light-sensing cells sit in the skin of every segment of your body, and they are most plentiful where your skin is most sensitive to light. In a flatworm called Schmidtea mediterranea, worms with their eyes removed or their heads cut off still shy away from near-ultraviolet light, so the skin and body sense it without eyes. Nobody has measured whether you sense light through your body in this way if you are any other kind of worm or leech.
rows.note: Left out any claim that all these worms lack eyes, since no record says so and some flatworms, fanworms and leeches have them.

rows.title: Bright and dim
rows.text: If you are a nightcrawler, you react negatively to light of ordinary brightness and move away from it. If you are a Mediterranean medicinal leech, the response of your S cell system to light depends strongly on how large an area is lit, and your adjustment to brightness happens locally. Nobody has measured how the other worms and leeches react to bright and dim light.
rows.note: Left out the nightcrawler's attraction to very dim light (R3 quote does not state it) and the planarian UV result (R2, Schmidtea is not a listed species or genus).

rows.title: A mole digging
rows.text: Picture a mole digging through the soil close to you. Nobody has measured whether you sense the shaking of that digging. The closest measurement is in the Mediterranean medicinal leech, where an abstract of nerve recordings proposes that a cell called the S cell detects water waves.
rows.note: Left out R2: its quote reports fewer earthworms near wind turbines, which does not state that earthworms sense vibration.

rows.title: Leeches
rows.text: If you are a Mediterranean medicinal leech, you have several eyes with pigment on your head, and light-sensing cells without pigment spread across your whole body. Nobody has recorded how many eyes the smooth turtle leech, the North American medicinal leech or the European medicinal leech have, so if you are one of those, your eye count is unknown.
rows.note: R1 says "several" head eyes with no count, so no number is given. The other three species have no eye-count record.

rows.title: Flatworms
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see, whether you are a hammerhead flatworm, a stripe-bellied flatworm or Schmidtea lugubris. A review of animal eyes lists one figure for a flatworm it calls Planaria, and that figure cannot be passed on to your genus.
rows.note: Left out numbers: R1's quote ("0.8 35 A") does not state 0.014 cycles per degree, and R2's quote gives 73° with no sign it is an acuity.

rows.title: Fan worms
rows.text: Your crown of feathery radioles has eyes on it. If you are an Indo-Pacific Christmas tree worm, the visual pigment in those eyes absorbs light best in the blue, at about 465 nanometers. If you are a Caribbean or California Christmas tree worm or a blue tube worm, you very likely have the same pigment, since all of you are close relatives in the same genus.
rows.note: Only the Indo-Pacific species is measured; the 465 nm figure is stated for it and the others are carried within the genus.

rows.title: Touch, taste and damp
rows.text: If you are a European medicinal leech, the touch-sensing cells in your body wall respond to stimulation repeated up to about 50 to 60 times a second, according to an abstract of an electrophysiology study. Nobody has measured how touch works in the other worms and leeches, so for them it is unknown.
rows.note: Only touch is supported; no records for taste or damp, so they are left out despite the title. Removed the year because it is not in the record.
